newsitem.title: USA: Dow index racks up second biggest daily gain ever.
newsitem.headline: Dow index racks up second biggest daily gain ever.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 179 points Tuesday -- just shy of setting a record single-day gain -- as new data calmed Wall Street's fears that the economy was growing at an inflationary pace.

The barometer of 30 blue-chip stocks rose 179.01 points, or 2.64 percent, to close at 6,962.03, its second largest gain after the 187-point rise that took place two days after the "Black Monday" stock crash of Oct. 19, 1987.
Last Tuesday, the index raced up 173 points but that gain also fell just short of the record one-day rise.
The buying frenzy was evident in the advance-decline ratio as 2,091 stocks rose while 527 fell on heavy volume of 547 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
In percentage terms, the Dow's gain was small in comparison with the rise of 187 points, or 10 percent, on Oct. 21, 1987, when the index closed at 2,027.85.

A smaller-than-expected increase in wage inflation and the largest drop since August 1996 in orders for manufactured goods, helped whet buyers' appetite for stocks in the wake of recent strong corporate earnings reports.
"You've got both portions of the equation working for you today," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line's Asset Management.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 25.60 points, or 2.1 percent, to 1,242.63. The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks jumped 21.09 points, or 2.7 percent, to 794.05.

The rally was just as explosive in the inflation-sensitive bond market, where the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond gained 1-17/32, sending its yield down to 6.98 percent from Monday's 7.11 percent. The last time the yield closed below 7 percent was on March 26, when it also settled at 6.98 percent.

Stocks rallied from the opening bell, keying off a surging bond market. Investors took heart in an small rise of only 0.6 percent in the Employment Cost Index for the first quarter. The data is closely watched by the Federal Reserve for signs of wage-led inflation.
Also helping sentiment was an unexpected drop of 3.0 percent in durable goods orders in March, the steepest drop since August 1996.

The reports lessened fears that the Fed would need to raise interest rates to cool the economy. The Fed raised short-term rates a quarter percentage point on March 25, leading to a month-long pullback that shaved nearly 10 percent from the Dow index.
"Many people feel the probability of the Fed tighting has been reduced," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at JP Morgan. "Our view is it's a bit premature to move in that direction."
The lower bond rates were making stocks more attractive, said Jonathan Dodd, technical analyst at Dean Witter.
"It's given people some room to play the market," he said.
The market's next economic data hurdle comes Wednesday morning with a report on first quarter gross domestic product.
Nevertheless, some analysts said Tuesday's rally suggested that the stock market's retreat had ended after the Dow's pullback from a record high close of 7,085.16 on March 11.
"We will get pauses to refresh but I think the correction is over," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
International Business Machines Corp. surged 8 to 158-3/8 after announcing a $3.5 billion addition to its stock buyback budget and a 14 percent dividend increase.
PepsiCo Inc. jumped 3-1/8 to 34-3/8 on stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings.
Building on solid gains seen on Monday, the stock of interest-rate sensitive banks rose sharply.
Chase Manhattan Corp. gained 2-3/4 to 90-1/2, Citicorp added 4-3/4 to 112, NationsBank Corp. was up 2-1/8 to 59-7/8, and Bank of New York jumped 2-3/4 to 39-7/8.
The American Stock Exchange index rose 6.83 to 548.03. The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 9.93 to 413.62. The average share was up 99 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,449.464 up 175.233 or 2.41 percent.
